status2026.detail:
The APS commissioning chart dated 5 October 2026 places 20-ID-D,E at stage 6, restart of the General User Program. The Proposal Types page dated 7 October 2026 lists both stations for regular and rapid-access General User proposals. Earlier charts show installation ongoing on 30 September 2024, installation complete on 16 December 2024 and in January 2025, operations commissioning on 10 March 2025, and scientific commissioning and early experiments from July 2025 through January 2026. In July 2025, Energy Secretary Chris Wright placed the inaugural sample, part of a jet-engine turbine blade, in the instrument. A July 2025 NSUF/APS report states that shielding verification occurred in 2025 and expected general users in late 2025 or early 2026. The exact first-light date is unpublished. The charts place it between late January and July 2025, probably by March if operations commissioning involved beam-on verification. That inference is unconfirmed. The September 2024 update had expected first light in that run, but the later charts indicate that it did not occur in 2024.

The Beamline Directory, reread on 9 October 2026, still lists 'Commissioning'. Its specifications assume a superconducting undulator and may be invalid during startup, estimated there at about a year. The insertion-device table, updated on 22 September 2026 and reread on 9 October, instead lists the interim upstream U21 and downstream U21/U25 revolver. The baseline pair of 1.9 m, 16.5 mm-period superconducting undulators was delayed by core-reliability problems. Installation is planned for 2026 to 2027. The Strategic Plan schedules 20-ID core fabrication through those years and commissioning near late 2027. Its May 2026 target for the first inline SCU at sector 1 had not been met by the September table, which lists no SCU at sector 1 or 20.

The adjacent Activated Materials Laboratory is operational. A Partner User Proposal allocates NSUF 690 hours per year shared between 1-ID and 20-ID, starting in run 2025-3. HEXM was absent from the August 2025 list of the last five feature beamlines awaiting operation.

tagline: Study grains, strain and cracks inside solid metal with high-energy X-rays, about 180 m from the source.
summary: With high-energy X-rays, scientists can study the interior of metal samples several millimetres thick. At the High-Energy X-ray Microscope, HEXM, photon energies range from 35 to 120 keV, or 35,000 to 120,000 electron-volts. Scientists measure structural changes during loading, heating or battery charging. The main sample position is about 180 m from the source in 20-ID-E, a room nearly 20 m long in the Long Beamline Building. The optical design includes wide illumination of whole samples and a focused spot about 200 nm tall for individual grains. Detectors are positioned from about a centimetre to 16 m behind the sample for measurements of grain rotation, strain and crack formation. Radioactive samples are prepared in the adjacent laboratory. General-user operations have begun with interim permanent-magnet undulators.

whatAPSUEnables.text: In the design brightness mode, the electron beam is about 19 times narrower horizontally, with a root-mean-square width of 14.7 µm rather than 280 µm. Vertical emittance, the beam size multiplied by its angular spread, decreases from about 40 to 4 pm·rad. At high photon energies, source size depends mainly on the electron beam because the intrinsic photon spread is small. With a source-to-sample distance of 180 m and focusing optics 2 m before the sample, the design focal spot is about 200 nm tall. The working distance leaves space for furnaces and load frames. Wider illumination of several millimetres is also possible. Before the upgrade, only about one photon in 100,000 at these energies was spatially coherent, insufficient for lens-free strain imaging within individual grains. At 40 keV, the design coherent flux is about 500 times the old 1-ID value. This projection assumes superconducting undulators that are not installed. No measured HEXM values are published.
quantitative: In design brightness mode, horizontal emittance decreases from 3,113 pm before the upgrade to 42 pm, about a factor of 74. Horizontal root-mean-square source width decreases from 280 to 14.7 µm.

The nominal design-lattice values at an insertion-device straight in flat-beam mode and at zero current are σx = 14.5 µm, σx′ = 2.75 µrad, σy = 3.08 µm and σy′ = 1.29 µrad. These are computed values, not measurements.
The coherent fraction at HEDM energies was about 10⁻⁵ before the upgrade, too low for high-energy coherent diffraction imaging.
At 40 keV, the projected gains over pre-upgrade 1-ID are about 500 in coherent flux and 150 in coherent fraction.

The smallest design focus at 20-ID-E is 0.43 × 0.21 µm full width at half maximum at 70 keV, with 4 × 10¹¹ photons per second. This uses L6 at f = 2 m. A vertical spot below 100 nm is projected with an f = 1 m kinoform.

The unfocused design beam is 2.5 × 2.2 mm full width at half maximum at 180 m and 70 keV. Illumination over several millimetres is possible with refractive expanders. Almer describes sample cross-sections increasing from about 1 mm to several millimetres.
The design SAXS minimum scattering vector is Qmin = 0.0007 Å⁻¹ at 40 keV, corresponding to dmax of about 870 nm. The observable size range is six times the 1-ID-E range.
Scattering-tomography resolution depends on beam size. The planned value is about 0.1 µm, compared with about 2 µm before the upgrade.

Compared with the pre-upgrade SCU1 at 1-ID, the planned superconducting source has 530 times the brilliance, 4.5 times the central-cone flux and 1.5 times the flux density, including the distance increase from 70 to 180 m.
Expected data rates are about 100 times those of 1-ID before the upgrade.

techniques.name: Far-field high-energy diffraction microscopy
techniques.text: Metals contain many small crystals, called grains. X-rays diffract into sharp spots when a grain is oriented at the required angle. For far-field high-energy diffraction microscopy, ff-HEDM or 3DXRD, scientists rotate a sample in a beam 1 to 2 mm wide and record patterns with a detector 0.5 to 1.5 m away. Software assigns spots to grains and calculates the position, orientation and full elastic strain of up to about 10,000 grains. Elastic strain describes stretching and compression in every direction. At pre-upgrade 1-ID-E, measured repeatability was about 5 µm in position, 0.02° in orientation and 2 × 10⁻⁴ in strain. Measurements at HEXM use both 20-ID-D and 20-ID-E.

techniques.name: Near-field high-energy diffraction microscopy
techniques.text: For near-field HEDM, nf-HEDM, a high-resolution detector is positioned 1 to 2 cm behind the sample. Diffraction spots then remain close to their originating grains. Scientists rotate and vertically translate the sample through a line beam less than a micrometre tall and ideally 3 to 4 mm wide, recording at several detector distances. Software fits grain shapes to the observed patterns through forward modelling. The result is a 3D map of grains and boundaries with about 1 µm spatial and 0.01° angular resolution. At HEXM, wide line illumination is obtained with diamond beam-expanding lenses and a long propagation distance.

techniques.name: Very-far-field high-energy diffraction microscopy
techniques.text: For very-far-field HEDM, vff-HEDM, the detector is at least 10 m behind the sample, up to about 16 m in 20-ID-E. Strain changes the spacing between atomic planes and therefore the angle of a diffraction spot. At high X-ray energies, these angular changes are small. At greater detector distances, each pixel corresponds to a smaller angular interval, allowing strain measurements within a grain. An energy spread of about 10⁻⁴ is required from the four-bounce monochromator to limit broadening caused by the beam's wavelength range.

techniques.name: Wide-angle scattering and pair distribution analysis
techniques.text: Wide-angle scattering, also called high-energy diffraction, produces rings from many grains illuminated at once. Scientists determine the crystal phases and their proportions, lattice strain, grain orientation and defect-related peak broadening. In pair distribution function analysis, PDF, scattering data at high angles are used to calculate the distribution of interatomic distances. Measurements use transmission geometry, with scattering angles below about 10 to 18°. For high-flux measurements, a whole undulator harmonic can be focused with white-beam lenses. The design bandwidth is 0.6%, with 4.8 × 10¹⁴ photons per second at 70 keV.

techniques.name: Scattering tomography
techniques.text: Scattering tomography combines diffraction measurements with computed tomography, CT. Scientists scan a narrow beam across a sample and rotate it, recording small- or wide-angle scattering at each position. Software reconstructs a 3D map of material composition, strain or nanostructure. Spatial resolution depends on beam size. The HEXM target is about 0.1 µm, compared with about 2 µm before the upgrade.

techniques.name: High-energy small-angle X-ray scattering
techniques.text: With high-energy small-angle X-ray scattering, HE-SAXS, scientists measure nanometre-scale voids, precipitates and fibres from X-rays scattered through small angles. These structures affect material strength. At a detector distance of about 14 m, the design minimum scattering vector is 0.0007 Å⁻¹ at 40 keV. This corresponds to structures up to about 870 nm, six times the old 1-ID-E range. The overlap with microscopy length scales allows measurements of the same voids or particles by scattering and direct imaging.

techniques.name: Micro-computed tomography
techniques.text: Micro-computed tomography, µCT, provides 3D images of pores, cracks and secondary phases in dense samples at micrometre resolution. Scientists record images of the illuminated field from multiple angles. A typical spatial resolution is about one thousandth of the beam width, so finer detail requires a smaller imaged volume. With an expanded white beam or single undulator harmonic, about 1 µm resolution is possible in a fraction of a second. Greater coherence strengthens phase contrast. In these images, edges are visible through changes in X-ray phase caused by refraction, as well as through absorption.

techniques.name: High-energy transmission X-ray microscopy
techniques.text: In transmission X-ray microscopy, TXM, a magnified image is formed through an X-ray lens after the sample and recorded about 15 m away. Optical magnification permits resolution finer than the detector pixel size at the sample. At the old 1-ID, about 500 nm resolution was achieved at 45 keV within a 6 m setup. The longer HEXM station permits greater magnification and depth of field, with a resolution target of about 100 nm.

techniques.name: High-energy Bragg coherent diffraction imaging
techniques.text: For Bragg coherent diffraction imaging, BCDI, scientists illuminate one buried grain with X-rays that have stable phase relationships across it. A 3D speckle pattern is recorded around a Bragg reflection. Software reconstructs grain shape and atomic displacement, from which strain is calculated. The goal is detail on the scale of tens of nanometres. The HEXM design uses a 48 × 31 µm coherent focus at 40 keV and an energy spread of 2 × 10⁻⁶ for grains about 10 to 20 µm across. Scientists select grains from an ff-HEDM map and record diffraction about 16 m away. A pre-upgrade proof of principle at 1-ID-E, using 52 keV X-rays, resolved structures of about 0.5 µm or smaller and strain of about 2.5 × 10⁻⁴.

techniques.name: Dark-field X-ray microscopy
techniques.text: For dark-field X-ray microscopy, DFXM, an objective lens is positioned in the beam diffracted by one grain. The resulting magnified image contains only that grain. Small changes in orientation and strain affect the local diffracted intensity, allowing measurements at sub-micrometre resolution inside bulk material. Ashley Bucsek described HEXM as the only beamline intended to offer DFXM at high energies. This remains a planned or emerging mode. No published HEXM result was found.

scienceCases.title: Dwell fatigue in turbine alloys
scienceCases.text: Repeated loading with long holds under stress can cause dwell fatigue in jet-engine materials. Titanium alloys are affected even at room temperature, while nickel superalloys are affected above about 700 °C. Scientists plan to map roughly a thousand grains under load and heat at HEXM, identify grains with high strain, and examine them with coherent imaging, dark-field microscopy or CT. These measurements would test whether some slip systems, the planes along which a crystal shears, creep slowly while others retain a low-temperature response. In July 2025, Energy Secretary Chris Wright placed the inaugural sample, a jet-engine turbine-blade section, in the instrument.

scienceCases.title: Irradiated nuclear materials
scienceCases.text: Steel and fuel exposed in nuclear reactors become radioactive, complicating laboratory study. At the Activated Materials Laboratory beside 20-ID-E, staff prepare and seal samples with dose rates up to 100 millirem per hour at 30 cm. The laboratory is funded through Nuclear Science User Facilities, NSUF. At HEXM, scientists measure cracks, voids and grain strain in 3D during heating and loading. NSUF has 690 hours of annual beamtime shared between 1-ID and 20-ID. More radioactive samples are intended mainly for 20-ID, outside the main hall. The first user experiment examined stainless steel after decades in a light-water reactor for evidence of irradiation-assisted stress-corrosion cracking. The report did not identify the beamline used.

scienceCases.title: Pores, stress and grains in 3D-printed metal
scienceCases.text: 3D-printed parts can contain small pores and residual stress left by processing. With large-field CT at HEXM, scientists plan to measure pore distributions in statistically useful volumes, with a resolution target of about 100 nm. Grain orientation and residual strain are measured through HEDM, and nanoscale precipitates through SAXS. Measurements during printing and welding are planned. Rapid analysis would help researchers select process settings for further experiments.

scienceCases.title: Stress and cracking in battery particles
scienceCases.text: Battery cathode particles contain crystals about 10 to 500 nm across. Uneven expansion as lithium enters and leaves can cause cracks along crystal boundaries after repeated charging. Planned HEXM measurements use nanofocused HEDM and coherent imaging to determine stress within individual crystals across many particles in full-size operating cells. A battery cycler is available for charging and discharging during measurements.

scienceCases.title: Strain in bone and natural composites
scienceCases.text: Bone contains protein fibres about 100 nm wide and mineral crystals. Scientists use small- and wide-angle scattering tomography to measure strain in each component under load. With the finer planned HEXM beam, spatial resolution should improve from about 2 µm toward 0.1 µm. For a given image quality in biological tissue, the lowest required dose occurs at about 60 to 100 keV, between the energy ranges dominated by photoelectric absorption and Compton scattering.

scienceCases.title: High-throughput grain mapping
scienceCases.text: Carnegie Mellon, Purdue, the University of Utah and the Colorado School of Mines built the high-throughput HEDM instrument with a National Science Foundation instrumentation grant. Carnegie Mellon led the project. A six-axis motorised stage provides sample rotation and translation for repeated grain-mapping measurements, with possible future mail-in access. The instrument was initially at 6-ID-D and moved to 20-ID-D in December 2023.

keyParameters.label: Monochromatic photon energy
keyParameters.note: The Beamline Directory gives 35 to 120 keV. The 2021 D3 detector-mover specification gives 35 to 140 keV for the photon delivery system. White-beam operation and focusing of individual broadband undulator harmonics are also specified.

keyParameters.label: White-beam operation
keyParameters.note: Staff withdraw the monochromators and lenses for white-beam operation.

keyParameters.label: Energy resolution ΔE/E
keyParameters.value: 10⁻³ with bent double-Laue optics. About 10⁻⁴ with four-bounce Si(111) optics, and 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁶ with high-order silicon reflections.
keyParameters.note: The AML report lists the optional high-resolution monochromator as ΔE/E of about 10⁻⁵.

keyParameters.label: Design unfocused flux at 70 keV in 20-ID-E
keyParameters.value: 10¹⁴ photons per second at 200 mA in the design brightness mode, with the planned SCU source
keyParameters.note: This design value assumes the 16.5 mm superconducting undulator. Flux with the interim permanent-magnet source is expected to be lower. The Strategic Plan estimates about three times greater brightness with SCUs than with hybrid permanent-magnet undulators above 50 keV. No measured 20-ID value is published.

keyParameters.label: Beam size range at sample
keyParameters.note: The FDR range is 0.43 × 0.21 µm with L6 at f = 2 m to 2.5 × 2.2 mm without focusing. The FDR Table 4.29 header gives µm for all rows, but the unfocused rows must be in mm, as confirmed by the Beamline Directory.

keyParameters.label: Optic-to-sample working distance
keyParameters.note: The FDR specifies focal lengths of 1 to 2 m for nanofocusing in 20-ID-E.

keyParameters.label: Design coherent beam for BCDI
keyParameters.value: 48 × 31 µm FWHM, 3.8 × 10⁹ ph/s at 40 keV, ΔE/E = 2 × 10⁻⁶
keyParameters.note: FDR Fig. 4.20 specifies L2 at 31 m and L5 at 76 m for this configuration.

keyParameters.label: Design focused beam from one broadband undulator harmonic
keyParameters.value: 182 × 47 µm in E or 50 × 13 µm in D, with 4.8 × 10¹⁴ photons per second and ΔE/E = 6 × 10⁻³ at 70 keV
keyParameters.note: The design includes focusing one full undulator harmonic, with 0.6% bandwidth, through diamond lenses L1. The estimated flux is four to five times the monochromatic flux. Beamline scientists call this pink beam. In this exhibit's legend, pink beam refers to a broad spectrum filtered by mirrors, which is a different configuration.

keyParameters.label: Source-to-sample distances
keyParameters.note: The 20-ID-E sample origin is 3.5 m downstream of the upstream wall, which is about 177.5 m from the source.

keyParameters.label: Beamline length to final stop
keyParameters.value: 197 m to the fixed white-beam stop
keyParameters.note: The 2020 groundbreaking release gives 180 m to the sample. Other descriptions give about 600 ft.

keyParameters.label: Maximum sample-to-detector distance
keyParameters.note: With detector D4 at about 197 m.

keyParameters.label: Diffraction-angle coverage
keyParameters.value: 2θ up to 18° for 1 Å d-spacing at 40 keV. Coverage is specified at 2 to 12 m with D3 and at the back wall with D4.

keyParameters.label: SAXS minimum Q
keyParameters.value: 0.0007 Å⁻¹ at 40 keV, corresponding to dmax of about 870 nm
keyParameters.note: Design estimate with D6 at 14 m and a 0.5 mm minimum radius.

keyParameters.label: Insertion devices in September 2026
keyParameters.value: Inline U21 with 21 mm period and 112 periods, and a U21/U25 revolver. U21 has Kmax = 1.38 and E1 = 8.36 keV.
keyParameters.note: These are interim devices. The baseline is two 1.9 m, 16.5 mm-period NbTi superconducting undulators in one 4.8 m cryostat.

keyParameters.label: Monochromator M1
keyParameters.value: LN2-cooled bent double-Laue Si(111), horizontal deflection, 25–35 mm outboard fixed offset
keyParameters.note: Built by Cinel and installed in 20-ID-A in January 2024; Si(111) per the Beamline Directory.

keyParameters.label: 20-ID-E interior dimensions
keyParameters.value: 19.8 m long. The upstream 11.3 m is 6.8 m wide and about 4.0 m high. The downstream section is 10.8 m wide and 6.9 m high.
keyParameters.note: Beam height is 1.4 m above the floor. Argonne described this as the largest enclosure built at the APS.

keyParameters.label: 20-ID-E stability environment
keyParameters.value: Expected temperature variation within ±0.05 °C over 24 hours, with a VC-E floor vibration standard
keyParameters.note: The HEXM enclosure floor slab is 12 in (30 cm) thick.

keyParameters.label: Front end
keyParameters.value: High-heat-load front end, with limits of 21 kW and 590 kW/mrad². A 2 mm horizontal × 1 mm vertical exit mask is at 25.4 m, and a 5 × 5 mm exit collimator at 26.1 m.

insertionDevices.name: APS21#5 (U21), upstream
insertionDevices.type: Planar hybrid permanent-magnet undulator outside the vacuum chamber
insertionDevices.notes: The upstream U21 has 112 periods and an 8.5 mm minimum device gap. At that gap, Keff = 1.38 and E1 = 8.36 keV for 6.0 GeV electrons at zero emittance. At 200 mA, power density is 216 kW/mrad² and total power 5.4 kW. Length is calculated as 112 × 21 mm. The Beamline Directory gives 2.3 m. This is the interim source as of 22 September 2026.

insertionDevices.name: APS21R25#9 revolver, U21/U25, downstream
insertionDevices.type: Planar hybrid permanent-magnet revolver undulator with two selectable magnetic structures
insertionDevices.notes: The first structure, APS21#14, has a 21 mm period, 112 periods, K = 1.38 and E1 = 8.32 keV. The second, APS25#11, has a 25 mm period, 94 periods, K = 1.98 and E1 = 4.61 keV, with 224 kW/mrad² power density and 8.0 kW total power. These are interim devices. The Beamline Directory lists the downstream source as U21.

insertionDevices.name: Baseline inline pair of 16.5 mm SCUs, uninstalled
insertionDevices.type: Two planar NbTi superconducting undulators in one 4.8 m cryostat
insertionDevices.notes: The APS-U baseline for sectors 1 and 20 is one pair per sector of inline 1.9 m, 16.5 mm-period superconducting undulators, with correctors inside the long cryostat. Core-reliability problems delayed installation, which is now planned for 2026 to 2027. FDR Section 4-4, 2019, specifies about 3.5 m total magnetic length, possibly 3.8 m, Kmax = 1.63 and 1.06 T at 8.0 mm gap. Design power through the 2 × 1 mm mask is 1.6 kW, with power density 600 kW/mrad². The PDR gives 17.9 kW total and 616 kW/mrad² at maximum field. A 2020 overview describes existing 1.1 m undulators and planned lengths up to 3.5 m. The 2025 to 2029 Strategic Plan, Fig. 8, schedules 20-ID core fabrication through 2026 and 2027 and commissioning near late 2027. The planned May 2026 installation of the first inline SCU at sector 1 had not occurred by the September insertion-device table, which lists no SCU at sector 1 or 20.

source.canting: There is no canting. The two devices are inline on one straight section. A phase shifter/corrector is between the permanent-magnet devices. In the SCU design, correctors are inside the cryostat.
source.frontEnd: The standard APS-U High Heat Load Front End is based on the 28-ID design. Its total power limit is 21 kW and peak power-density limit 590 kW/mrad². It contains the clearing magnet, burn-through fixed mask BTFM1, GRID XBPM1, photon shutter with intensity monitor, safety shutters and exit mask with XBPM2. The 20-ID window-exit configuration has a 2 mm horizontal × 1 mm vertical mask at 25.4 m and a 5 × 5 mm tungsten collimator at 26.1 m. Window material is inconsistent in the FDR. Section 4-4.3 specifies 0.5 mm beryllium, while Table 4.28 specifies diamond.
source.sourceSizeAndDivergence: The electron-beam sizes and divergences at the insertion-device straight are zero-current APS-U design-lattice calculations. They are not measurements. In flat-beam mode at κ = 0.1, used for the brightness-mode design, σx = 14.47 µm, σx′ = 2.75 µrad, σy = 3.08 µm and σy′ = 1.29 µrad. In round-beam mode, used for the timing-mode design, the corresponding values are 12.3 µm, 2.34 µrad, 8.26 µm and 3.47 µrad. The FDR Table 1.1 brightness-mode values are 14.7 µm, 2.8 µrad, 3.2 µm and 1.3 µrad in that order. For a 2.35 m undulator at 70 keV, the photon contribution calculated here is about 0.7 µm size and 1.9 µrad divergence. Including it gives photon-source sizes of about 14.5 × 3.2 µm and divergences of 3.4 × 2.3 µrad rms before energy-spread broadening. That broadening is substantial at the 7th to 13th harmonics used at HEXM. FDR Fig. 4.20 uses horizontal and vertical FWHM source sizes of 35 and 9 µm for the BCDI optics design. The PDR also gives 9 µm vertical FWHM.

branches.name: 20-ID (single branch)
branches.description: One straight beamline with no net horizontal deflection. The bent Laue monochromator displaces the monochromatic beam about 25–35 mm outboard, parallel to the white-beam axis. White or monochromatic beam goes to 20-ID-D (about 70 m) or, through a movable stop, on to 20-ID-E (about 180 m) in the Long Beamline Building.

components.name: Upstream undulator U21 (APS21#5)
components.distanceNote: The two 2.35 m devices are inline on the straight section, with estimated centres near ±1.3 m relative to the source origin at 0 m.
components.text: Electrons emit X-rays as they change direction repeatedly between alternating magnetic poles. Radiation from successive bends interferes to produce a narrow, bright beam. The first HEXM undulator is a 2.35 m permanent-magnet device with 224 alternating magnets. Its fundamental energy is 8.36 keV at minimum gap and increases as the gap opens. Higher harmonics are used at HEXM, with 35 keV on the third, 70 keV near the seventh and 120 keV on the 11th to 13th. This is an interim device pending superconducting-undulator installation.

components.name: Downstream revolver undulator U21/U25 (APS21R25#9)
components.distanceNote: The illustrated position is approximate, as for the upstream device.
components.text: With both undulators, the flux is roughly twice that of one device alone. This revolver undulator has selectable 21 mm and 25 mm magnet arrays on a rotating mount. The directory identifies the 21 mm array as the source. A phase shifter between the devices adjusts the phase relationship of their radiation. Both undulators are interim. The baseline replacement is two 1.9 m superconducting undulators with 16.5 mm periods in one 4.8 m cryostat, planned for 2026 to 2027.

specs.baseline replacement: 2 × 1.9 m, 16.5 mm NbTi SCU in a 4.8 m cryostat

components.name: High-heat-load front end (shutters, masks, XBPMs)
components.distanceNote: Schematic placement inside the storage-ring tunnel. The front end ends at the ratchet wall at about 25.4–26.1 m; exact internal positions are not published.
components.text: The front end is inside the concrete-shielded accelerator tunnel. Unwanted X-ray power is absorbed in masks, beam position is measured with monitors, and the beam can be interrupted by shutters in a fraction of a second. The standard APS-U high-heat-load design is rated for 21 kW. At minimum gap, the two undulators provide about 10.8 kW.

components.name: Front-end exit mask and window
components.distanceNote: Position from FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: The front-end exit opening is 2 mm wide and 1 mm tall, half the standard mask height. Only the central X-ray cone passes through, limiting heat on downstream optics. A window separates the accelerator and beamline vacuums. The design documents specify either 0.5 mm beryllium or diamond, and the installed material is unconfirmed.

specs.window: The FDR text gives 0.5 mm beryllium, while the table gives diamond. The installed material is unconfirmed.

components.name: Front-end exit collimator
components.distanceNote: Position from FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: The X-ray beam passes through a 5 mm square opening in a tungsten block. Bremsstrahlung outside the opening is absorbed. This very-high-energy radiation is emitted when accelerator electrons strike gas or metal.

components.name: White-beam filters F1 (20ID-FL-1)
components.distanceNote: Position from FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: Low-energy X-rays are absorbed in thin diamond and silicon sheets before the monochromator. More than 85% of the useful 40 keV X-rays pass through. Absorbed power is under 100 W per sheet. With these filters and the slits, the first monochromator crystal receives about 55 to 60 W, within the capacity of liquid-nitrogen cooling.

components.name: High-heat-load white-beam slits S1 (20ID-SL-1)
components.distanceNote: Position from FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: The beam opening between cooled tungsten-edged jaws is usually no larger than 0.6 mm square, with a maximum of 2 mm. At 70 keV, this includes the central cone with broadening due to the electron energy spread. Radiation outside the opening is absorbed as heat.

components.name: L1 white-beam diamond refractive lenses
components.distanceNote: Position from FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: In the design, diamond lenses are placed before monochromatic energy selection. Focal distance depends on photon energy, so the full white beam does not have one sharp focus. An individual undulator harmonic, with about 0.6% energy bandwidth, can be focused. The design flux is 4.8 × 10¹⁴ photons per second at 70 keV, four to five times the narrow-band monochromatic value. The design also includes manual exchange of the lens stacks for beam expansion to several millimetres during imaging.

components.name: M1 high-energy bent double-Laue monochromator (20ID-MN-1)
components.distanceNote: Position from FDR Table 4.28. In the 3D model, the two crystals are 0.53 m apart. This is calculated as 30 mm/tan(2θB) for a 30 mm offset at 70 keV. The white-beam stop is between them on the white-beam axis.
components.text: An X-ray energy between 35 and 120 keV is selected at two bent silicon crystals, with about 0.1% energy spread. Diffraction occurs through the crystals in Laue geometry, at about 1.6° to the atomic planes at 70 keV. Bending increases angular acceptance. The predecessor at 1-ID provided more than ten times the flux of flat crystals. Distortion from the first crystal is compensated at the second. Deflection is horizontal, preserving the small vertical beam size and angular spread. The monochromatic beam is parallel to the incident beam, with a 25 to 35 mm lateral offset. Liquid-nitrogen cooling is used. The monochromator was installed in January 2024.

components.name: Diamond window (20ID-WN-1)
components.distanceNote: Position from FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: A thin diamond window separates the first beamline vacuum section from the next. This section extends from the front-end window through the monochromator. Absorption of high-energy X-rays in the diamond is low.

components.name: L2 collimating lenses
components.distanceNote: Position from FDR Table 4.28. The lenses were outside project scope in that design.
components.text: Beam divergence is reduced at collimating lenses with about 31 m focal length in the coherent-imaging configuration. A nearly parallel beam is needed because the next monochromator accepts a narrow angular range. In a 2026 paper, diamond collimating lenses were reported on a long beamline, presumed to be HEXM. Their use here is not confirmed. Like most HEXM lenses, they were outside the upgrade project scope.

specs.f: About 31 m in the BCDI configuration

components.name: M2 high-resolution four-bounce monochromator (20ID-MN-2)
components.distanceNote: Position from FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: With the optional second monochromator, the energy spread is reduced by a further factor of 10 to 1,000 for very-far-field strain measurements and coherent imaging. Four flat silicon crystals form a +−−+ reflection sequence, with vertical deflection and zero net offset. Si(111) gives about 10⁻⁴ relative energy spread. Higher-order reflections give 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁶ for coherent imaging of grains about 10 µm across. The crystal pairs are on flexure mounts in air, following a design tested at 1-ID.

components.name: Attenuators F2 and calibration foils F3

components.text: Staff insert metal foils on rotating wheels to reduce beam intensity or calibrate photon energy. Calibration uses elemental absorption edges, the energies above which absorption increases sharply. During long measurements, energy drift is checked against the same edges. components.distanceNote: Position estimated from FDR Fig. 4.19, between foils F3 and lenses L3. It is absent from Table 4.28.

components.distanceNote: Position from FDR Table 4.28, where the lenses are outside project scope. The PDR gives about 34 m.
components.text: With L3, the design focus is 155 × 40 µm at 20-ID-E and 70 keV. components.distanceNote: Position from FDR Table 4.28.

components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.28 gives positions of 66.2, 66.5 and 66.8 m.

components.name: Multi-beam slits S3 (20ID-SL-3)
components.distanceNote: Position from FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: Motorised slits define the beam opening. A small aperture is used as a secondary source for more stable downstream focusing. The opening also determines transverse coherence by selecting a narrower part of the beam.

components.name: Fast shutter (20ID-FS-1)
components.distanceNote: Position from FDR Table 4.28.

components.name: L4 short-focal-length focusing optics
components.distanceNote: Position from FDR Table 4.28. The lenses were outside project scope in that design.

A 230 nm focus at 51 keV was achieved in tests at 1-ID.

components.distanceNote: Position from FDR Table 4.28.

components.name: High-throughput HEDM instrument (20-ID-D)
components.distanceNote: Position of instrument 20ID-BI-1 from FDR Table 4.28. The model depicts 20-ID-D without a sample, with the beam continuing to 20-ID-E. This is an illustrative operating configuration.
components.text: The high-throughput grain-mapping instrument was built by four universities with National Science Foundation funding. Sample rotation and translation use a six-axis motorised stage for repeated measurements. The instrument moved from 6-ID-D in December 2023. components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.28 gives an extent of 72.5 to 75 m. The illustrated detector is moved 0.7 m inboard, clear of the beam continuing to 20-ID-E.

components.distanceNote: Position from FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: S5 defines the aperture for the beam continuing to 20-ID-E. For coherent imaging, a central part of the beam with stable phase relationships across it is selected before L5.

components.distanceNote: Position from FDR Table 4.28. The lenses were outside project scope in that design.

components.distanceNote: Position from FDR Table 4.28. The stop is drawn raised for beam transport to 20-ID-E.
components.text: With this cooled stop inserted, white or monochromatic beam is absorbed here. Measurements can then proceed in 20-ID-D while staff work in 20-ID-E. With the stop withdrawn, X-rays continue to the far station.

components.name: Long shielded transport ST-2 (hall to Long Beamline Building)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.28 gives the extent as 77.0 to 177.5 m.

components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.28 places the window at 177.7 m and temporary slits at 178.2 m.

components.name: Beam-conditioning optics table with L6 nano-focusing lenses
components.distanceNote: L6 position is from FDR Table 4.28. The estimated table extent is about 178 to 180 m.

components.name: Sample position: HR-SMS, HL-SMS and RAMS load frame
components.distanceNote: Position of instrument 20ID-BI-3 from FDR Table 4.28. ESD-010 places the sample origin 3.5 m from the upstream wall and 1.4 m above the floor. Rail, truss and cart dimensions are illustrative.

The high-resolution stage is a hexapod with a rotation stage on top. The high-load cart has guide columns for load frames. Scientists apply tension, torsion, heat or charge cycles during X-ray measurements, using equipment including the RAMS rotational and axial load frame, a radio-frequency furnace and a battery cycler.

components.name: D1 near-field / imaging detector
components.distanceNote: The PDR places the detector 1 to 2 cm downstream of the sample for near-field HEDM and farther downstream for CT. The illustrated position is retracted about 0.1 m outboard for far-field measurements.
components.text: Near-field grain mapping and CT use a high-resolution detector 1 to 2 cm behind the sample. X-rays are converted to visible light in a thin scintillator crystal. A reflected, magnified image of that light is recorded with a camera, giving about 1 µm resolution. Above 40 keV, fewer than 10% of incident X-rays are absorbed in such thin screens, so detector efficiency remains a development problem.

components.name: D2 detector system (near far-field WAXS/HEDM)
components.distanceNote: The estimated position is about 1 m downstream of the sample, based on the PDR and poster. In the illustrated far-field configuration, it is moved about 0.8 m inboard, clear of the direct beam.
components.text: Wide-angle patterns and far-field grain maps are recorded with a flat-panel detector about a metre behind the sample. It is mounted on a six-leg hexapod. In the rendered configuration, it is displaced from the beam for measurements with the more distant detectors.

components.name: L7 TXM objective (direct or diffracted beam)
components.distanceNote: The PDR places L7 after the sample, and the poster includes a TXM objective stand in the downstream hutch. The exact distance is unpublished. The objective is illustrated lowered clear of the beam.
components.text: A magnified X-ray image is formed through an objective lens after the sample and recorded at the back of the station. In the direct beam, the method is transmission microscopy, with a target resolution of about 100 nm. In the beam diffracted by one grain, it is dark-field microscopy and the image contains that grain only. Far-field patterns can also be relayed to the back-wall detectors through this optic.

components.name: D3 detector manipulation system (2–12 m WAXS / HEDM)
components.distanceNote: ESD-010 gives longitudinal rail limits at Z = 183 and 193 m. FDR Table 4.28 gives 183.3 to 192.5 m. The listed position is the upstream travel limit. The model depicts a detector on the outboard rail 6 m from the sample, at a Debye ring angle of 2θ = 8°. This is an illustrative configuration.
components.text: A 100 kg detector is positioned on a floor-rail tower 2 to 12 m behind the sample, with metre-scale horizontal and vertical travel. The coverage is a 36° cone, or scattering angles up to 18°, corresponding to 1 Å atomic-plane spacings at 40 keV. Position repeatability must be within 75 µm, with drift below 15 µm per day. Position is measured by a laser tracker. The reference detector in the specification is a Pilatus3 X CdTe 6M. The earlier robot-arm concept was replaced by this tower.

specs.travel: At least 5 m horizontal × 3.5 m vertical × 9.5 m longitudinal
specs.reference detector: Pilatus3 X CdTe 6M, with 172 µm pixels

components.name: D6 SAXS detector
components.distanceNote: The PDR places the detector about 14 m from the sample. In ESD Fig. 2, the SAXS table is near the back wall. Its illustrated position is approximate.
components.text: Small-angle scattering is recorded about 14 m behind the sample to measure nanometre-scale pores and particles. The design minimum scattering vector is 0.0007 Å⁻¹ at 40 keV, corresponding to structures up to about 870 nm. The design concept specifies a photon-counting detector.

components.name: D5 TXM imaging detector
components.distanceNote: The PDR places the detector about 15 m from the sample. D5 and D6 are on the same axis near the back wall. The illustrated D5 is moved 1.3 m inboard.
components.text: The magnified microscopy image is recorded about 15 m from the sample. High spatial resolution and detection efficiency are required at high X-ray energies. A vendor reports amorphous-selenium detectors with 8 µm pixels designed into the beamline, without identifying their position.

specs.candidate: KA Imaging BrillianSe amorphous-selenium detector with 8 µm pixels, according to the vendor

components.name: D4 back-wall detector system (BCDI / vff-HEDM)
components.distanceNote: ESD-010 places the detector at approximately 197 m. The model depicts a back-wall detector 2.3 m off axis, at one Bragg spot at 2θ = 8°. This is an illustrative configuration.
components.text: At the back wall, about 16 m from the sample, detector position is adjusted across the diffraction pattern. The long distance permits small angular changes and single-grain speckle to be resolved. The upper half of a 17.8° diffraction cone is accessible, including opposite-reflection pairs, called Friedel pairs. For sufficient coherent-fringe sampling, detector resolution must be 5 µm or better, with high efficiency and a wide intensity range. This remains a development goal.

specs.resolution requirement: At most 5 µm, with high efficiency and a wide intensity range. This is a research and development requirement.

Samples are positioned on a six-axis Aerotech stage. Four universities led by Carnegie Mellon built the instrument with a National Science Foundation instrumentation grant, with about $1.09 million obligated. It was moved to HEXM in December 2023. Two sample stages are interchangeable, with detector distances from 1 to 2 cm up to 16 m. Final focusing optics are on the beam-conditioning table. The high-resolution hexapod stage and high-load cart for load frames are on floor rails below an overhead truss. Detector positions are measured with a laser tracker. Six detector systems are specified for near-field measurements with D1, far-field measurements with D2 and D3, back-wall measurements with D4, microscopy with D5 and small-angle scattering with D6. The temperature-stability target is ±0.05 °C over 24 hours, and the floor vibration standard is VC-E.

instruments.name: Activated Materials Laboratory (support facility)
instruments.text: Staff prepare radioactive samples in the adjacent Activated Materials Laboratory, using fume hoods, shielded glove boxes and equipment for sealing samples in containers. The Department of Energy's Nuclear Science User Facilities program, NSUF, funded the laboratory. The accepted dose-rate limit is 100 millirem per hour at 30 cm. Staff transfer samples to 1-ID and 20-ID. A partner user proposal allocates NSUF 690 hours of beamtime each year.

geometryNotes:
HEXM follows one line from the 20-ID straight section to the fixed stop at 197 m, with no net angular deflection in the horizontal plane. At 29.5 m, the bent double-Laue M1 monochromator produces a parallel beam displaced 25 to 35 mm outboard. The white-beam path is on axis. The four-bounce M2 has zero net offset. The beam is tangent to the ring at sector 20, at a slight angle to neighbouring lines. ISN at 19-ID starts about 2 m inboard but is rotated 9° outboard. In the Long Beamline Building, ISN is therefore on the outboard side of HEXM. Outboard is left when looking downstream, the APS +X direction in ESD-010. In site.json coordinates, the 20-ID direction is 168.8° and the 19-ID direction 177.8°.

Inside the hall, 20-ID-A is against the ratchet wall at about 26 to 36 m. Shielded transport passes through the unused legacy 20-ID-B and 20-ID-C hutches near 50 to 65 m, then reaches the new 20-ID-D near 65 to 77 m. This is near the downstream limit of the hall.

The roughly 100 m ST-2 pipe crosses the experiment-floor walkway. Stairs and an elevator provide access over it. The pipe passes through lab-office Building 436, where offices were removed, and along a new office corridor into Building 444, the Long Beamline Building.

The lead-shielded 20-ID-E hutch has two roof heights. Its upstream section is 6.8 m wide and about 4 m high, with a roof walkway. The downstream section from about 188.8 m is 10.8 m wide and 6.9 m high. For 1 Å d-spacing at 40 keV, 2θ = 17.8°. At a detector distance of 16.4 m, the cone radius is tan(17.8°) × 16.4 m = 5.3 m. That fits within the 5.4 m distance to a side wall and 5.5 m from beam height to the ceiling. The back-wall D4 detector is about 16 m from the sample. Beam height is 1.4 m above the floor.

The poster includes an overhead truss across the sample area and tall tan D3 and D4 detector movers labelled HEXM. The Activated Materials Laboratory is on the inboard side of 20-ID-E. The 2019 design places the control room and sample preparation on the outboard side.

In the Strategic Plan photograph, the external building sections are the low Activated Materials Laboratory, tall HEXM hutch and ISN section in that order.

The FDR Fig. 4.1 caption states that the beam travels left to right, but the ring is on the right and the Long Beamline Building on the left. The correct beam direction in that drawing is right to left. In that orientation, HEXM is inboard of ISN and the laboratory inboard of HEXM. This agrees with Fig. 4.18, where the beam travels left to right, with the control room and sample preparation above the beam on the outboard side and the laboratory below on the inboard side.

interactiveIdeas.title: Measurements at different length scales
interactiveIdeas.concept: Start with a jet-engine turbine blade and change the displayed length scale in powers of ten. Show the technique and detector distance on the hutch model at each scale. Include CT at millimetre scales with resolution about beam size/1000, near-field HEDM grain maps at micrometre scales, far-field HEDM strain per grain, BCDI or DFXM within one grain at tens of nanometres, and WAXS or PDF atomic spacings below 1 Å.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Explain why several measurements are needed to study a material over seven orders of magnitude in length scale. Use each measurement to choose a region for finer-scale study.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Direct-imaging resolution is approximately beam size/1000. Grain-resolved HEDM is practical for up to about 10⁴ illuminated grains. Near-field HEDM resolves about 1 µm and 0.01°. Far-field HEDM measures strain per grain to about 2 × 10⁻⁴. BCDI resolves tens of nanometres, with strain sensitivity near 10⁻⁴. Keep 2θ below about 10 to 18° at energies of 35 to 120 keV.

interactiveIdeas.title: Photon energy and transmission
interactiveIdeas.concept: Change photon energy from 10 to 120 keV for slabs of aluminium, titanium, steel, nickel superalloy and tungsten. Display transmitted intensity and attenuation length. Include a turbine blade, battery and reactor-fuel pellet as sample examples.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Relate photon energy to transmission through full-size metal parts and their containment.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Use NIST mass attenuation coefficients and I/I₀ = exp(−(µ/ρ)ρt). The iron 1/e attenuation length is about 7 µm at 10 keV, 0.35 mm at 40 keV, 1.5 mm at 70 keV and 3.4 mm at 100 keV. Tungsten and uranium absorb strongly. The laboratory report gives penetration near 100 µm at 70 keV and above. Calculated NIST values range from about 0.03 to 0.25 mm over 40 to 120 keV, with discontinuities at the tungsten K edge of 69.5 keV and uranium K edge of 115.6 keV. Display the tungsten discontinuity. Attenuation does not vary linearly with energy.

interactiveIdeas.title: Optical distance and focal spot size
interactiveIdeas.concept: Move a lens along the beam between station D near 70 m and station E near 180 m, and choose its focal length. Display source demagnification, chromatic blur and diffraction contributions to spot size. Compare historical brightness and timing source modes. Include a separate beam-expansion configuration.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Relate optical distance to spot size, working distance and broad uniform illumination for whole-sample imaging.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Use 1/f = 1/p + 1/q. The demagnified FWHM size is 2.355σ(source)q/p. Add FWHM contributions in quadrature. At 180 m, f = 2 m and 70 keV, vertical contributions of 99, 152 and 104 nm give 209 nm, from FDR Table 4.30. For CRLs, f = R/(2Nδ). The diamond δ at 70 keV, calculated from electron density, is about 1.5 × 10⁻⁷. For R = 50 µm and f = 2 m, N is about 84. Focal length scales as E² because δ is proportional to λ². Chromatic blur therefore depends on ΔE/E. Kinoform apertures are larger than CRL apertures.

interactiveIdeas.title: Detector distance and diffraction information
interactiveIdeas.concept: Rotate a polycrystalline sample and move the detector between a near-field distance of 1 cm, far-field distance of 1 m and very-far-field distance of 15 m. Display the changes in spot separation, spatial information and strain resolution. Apply a load and display the resulting spot shifts.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Explain which information can be obtained at each detector distance. Relate the very-far-field configuration to the 20 m hutch length.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Use Bragg's law, λ = 2d sin(θ), with λ in Å equal to 12.398 divided by energy in keV. For Fe(110) at 70 keV, 2θ is about 5.0°. Strain is Δd/d = −cot(θ)Δθ, and angular resolution is about pixel size divided by detector distance. Near-field measurements at 1 to 2 cm give spatial maps. Far-field measurements give grain averages.

interactiveIdeas.title: Coherence and single-grain speckle
interactiveIdeas.concept: Compare old-APS and APS-U source sizes and display the coherent area at 180 m. Illuminate one grain and display its 3D speckle pattern. Change detector pixel size to show undersampling. Change bandwidth to show the loss of fringe contrast above ΔE/E of about 10⁻⁵.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Relate high-energy coherent imaging to source size, narrow bandwidth and detector distance.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: In the Gaussian Schell model, rms transverse coherence length is ξ = λz/(2πσ). At 40 keV and 180 m, the calculated horizontal value is about 60 µm for APS-U with σx = 14.5 µm, compared with 3 µm for the old APS with σx = 280 µm. Definitions differ by factors near two. Longitudinal coherence is approximately λ/(2ΔE/E). At 40 keV, λ = 0.31 Å, giving about 15 nm at ΔE/E = 10⁻³, 1.5 µm at 10⁻⁵ and 7.8 µm at 2 × 10⁻⁶. Some definitions use λ²/Δλ, twice these lengths. Detector fringe period is λL/D. For D = 10 µm and L = 16 m at 40 keV, it is about 50 µm. Pixels must therefore be 25 µm or smaller. The designed coherent focus is 48 × 31 µm in FDR Fig. 4.20.

interactiveIdeas.title: Undulator harmonics
interactiveIdeas.concept: Select the interim U21 or planned 16.5 mm superconducting undulator and change K through gap or current. Plot odd harmonics over 35 to 120 keV, with harmonic overlap and brilliance at the selected energy.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Explain the use of high undulator harmonics at high photon energies. Compare photon output with shorter magnetic periods and stronger superconducting fields.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Use Eₙ[keV] = n × 0.9496 Eₑ[GeV]² / (λu[cm](1 + K²/2)), with Eₑ = 6.0 GeV. For U21, E1 = 8.36 keV at K = 1.38. The calculated 7th harmonic reaches 70 keV at K near 1.1. Only odd harmonics occur on axis. Include broadening from the 0.136% electron energy spread at high harmonics, using the Tanaka–Kitamura correction dependent on nNσE. The planned SCU brilliance gain over the pre-upgrade SCU1 is 530-fold.

interactiveIdeas.title: Hutch dimensions and the diffraction cone
interactiveIdeas.concept: Display a cutaway of 20-ID-E and the Debye cone for 1 Å spacing at 40 keV. Show its intersection with the wide, tall downstream section and D4 back wall. Change energy and spacing to display the resulting cone angles.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Relate the downstream dimensions of 10.8 m wide and 6.9 m tall to coverage of an approximately 18° diffraction cone.

interactiveIdeas.concept: Show a reactor component, shipping cask, laboratory glove box, encapsulation, transfer cart, HEDM scan in 20-ID-E and sample return. Display dose-rate readings at each step.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Explain sample containment, preparation and transfer for measurements of irradiated materials.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: The dose-rate limit is 100 mrem per hour for beta and gamma radiation at 30 cm. Require at least one containment layer. Containment must transmit sufficient X-rays at 60 to 100 keV. The 1/e attenuation length in steel and zirconium is of the order of millimetres. Higher-dose samples are preferentially measured at 20-ID outside the main hall.

funFacts: At about 20 m long, 20-ID-E was described by Argonne as the largest enclosure built at the APS.
The main HEXM station is in the Long Beamline Building. Groundbreaking took place on 22 July 2020. Argonne described the building as the only externally visible part of the APS Upgrade.
The sample is about 180 m, or 590 ft, from the source. This is about 2.3 times a more typical 80 m distance. The calculated X-ray travel time is about 0.6 microseconds.
Construction required the removal of offices in lab-office Building 436 and a new corridor with 14 offices along the beam pipe.
The long beamlines cross the walkway around the APS ring at sectors 19 and 20. Stairs and an elevator provide access over the pipes. A complete lap on the original walkway is no longer possible.
The downstream part of 20-ID-E is 10.8 m wide and 6.9 m tall. X-rays scattered at 18° are measured at the back-wall detector about 16 m from the sample.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright placed the inaugural HEXM sample, part of a jet-engine turbine blade, in July 2025.
Four universities built the high-throughput HEDM instrument for 20-ID-D with National Science Foundation funding.

Before HEXM, sector 20 was used for X-ray spectroscopy for more than 25 years, with about 600 published papers. That program moved to 25-ID in 2022. The Pacific Northwest Consortium CAT was formed in 1990.
The HEXM hutch is on a 12 in concrete slab. The neighbouring ISN slab is 39 in thick for vibration control.
In the adjacent laboratory, the first users studied radioactive stainless-steel parts removed from a nuclear reactor after decades of service.
Before the upgrade, only about one in 100,000 photons at HEDM energies was spatially coherent. High-energy coherent imaging was therefore impractical.
Ashley Bucsek of the University of Michigan described high-energy dark-field X-ray microscopy as a planned capability unique to HEXM. Its operational status is unconfirmed.
The design specifies detector-position measurements with a Leica Absolute Tracker-class laser tracker. The detectors weigh about 100 kg.

openQuestions: The exact first-light date is unpublished. Monthly charts show installation complete in December 2024 and January 2025, operations commissioning on 10 March 2025, and scientific commissioning and early experiments by July 2025. The July 2025 laboratory report places shielding verification in 2025. These records imply first light between late January and July 2025, most likely by March. The latter date is an inference.

The 5 October 2026 commissioning chart shows general-user operation, and the Proposal Types page lists 20-ID-D,E for General User proposals. The Beamline Directory still says 'Commissioning' and may be outdated.

As of 22 September 2026, the interim source is an upstream permanent-magnet U21 and downstream U21/U25 revolver. The SCU baseline changed from about 3.5 to 3.8 m total magnetic length at Kmax = 1.63 in FDR Section 4-4 to two 1.9 m devices in one cryostat in Chapter 3 and the Strategic Plan. Installation is planned for 2026 to 2027 after core-reliability problems. The directory flux of 10¹⁴ photons per second at 70 keV assumes the SCU. It has not been measured with the interim source.
The installed front-end window material is unconfirmed. FDR Section 4-4.3 and the Table 4.27 note specify 0.5 mm beryllium, while Table 4.28 specifies diamond.

The installed L1 to L7 refractive optics are unclear as of 2026. The FDR lists most lens sets as research and development outside project scope. The July 2025 laboratory report confirms refractive focusing optics in 20-ID-A without details. The Shastri and Antipov JSR 2026 abstract, available through Europe PMC, describes diamond lenses for collimation before a high-resolution monochromator, coherent-diffraction focusing on a long beamline and a convex beam-expander test at 40 to 70 keV. The full text was inaccessible because of Cloudflare. Lens positions, focal lengths and the beamline used are unverified.

The installed detector suite is unclear. The directory lists Varex 4343 and SpectrumLogic 3131HS without a station. The D3 specification uses Pilatus3 X CdTe 6M as its reference. KA Imaging states that BrillianSe amorphous-selenium detectors are included at 20-ID. D4 specification ESD-011 is unpublished, and SpectrumLogic 3131HS specifications could not be verified.
User access to BCDI and DFXM is unconfirmed. The laboratory report lists BCDI at 20-ID-E, but no published HEXM BCDI or DFXM result was found.
The 2017 PDR XMAT ion-irradiation source, requiring 20 to 30 m of space beside the C/E station, is absent from later documents. Whether it was built is unconfirmed.

The 20-ID-A, B, C and D enclosure extents were scaled from the 2019 FDR layout, with about ±0.5 m uncertainty. Installed extents may differ. The 20-ID-E dimensions are from the 2021 ESD and agree with the 64 ft 11 in × 35 ft 5 in dimensions in FDR Fig. 4.1.
FDR Table 4.28 places the sample at 180.7 m. ESD-010 implies about 180.9 m, with the sample 3.5 m from an upstream wall near 177.4 m.
The upper energy limit is 120 keV in the FDR and directory, but 140 keV in the D3 photon-delivery specification.
The 2017 PDR uses station names A, B and C. The FDR and installed line use 20-ID-A, D and E. Legacy 20-ID-B and C remain in the hall without operations.
The February 2026 DOE article does not identify whether the first laboratory user experiment was at 1-ID or 20-ID.
FDR Table 4.29 labels every beam-size row in µm. The unfocused values of 2.5 × 2.2 at E and 1 × 0.9 at D must be mm, as confirmed by the directory.

The 3D model depicts far-field HEDM at 70 keV in 20-ID-E. At 20-ID-D, no sample is mounted and the detector is aside. Real operation alternates between stations. The movable stop is closed for independent 20-ID-D operation.
